transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-02 10:00 PST; duration 45m; attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Rachel (Nimbus Dir ML), Marcus (Nimbus Infra), Priya (PM)

[00:00] Sophie: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, we'll do a quick agenda - perf recap, tuning notes, next steps. Rachel you had asked about continuous batching behaviour after last run?
[00:14] Rachel: Yeah thanks, short on time today but wanted to see the numbers you mentioned in the doc. We saw a lot of throughput variance and some p99 spikes around the 400ms mark which is above our SLO.
[00:29] Daniel: Right, so quick recap: last Friday we ran the 30 minute steady-state with H100s, model variant quant-8 and we tuned the batching window to 20ms. Average tokens/sec looked good ~11k tokens/sec per GPU, but we did see p95 at ~120ms and p99 closer to 420ms in bursts.
[00:46] Marcus: Just to be clear, that 11k is with the prefix caching enabled? We thought KV cache was off for some of those runs.
[00:58] Daniel: Good catch, for the Friday run KV caching was partially enabled - some trace routing caused misses so effective caching was around 60%. That explains the variance.
[01:12] Rachel: Okay, makes sense. Our traffic has a long tail of short and long sequences so cache hit-rate is important. We need consistent p99 under 300ms ideally.
[01:26] Sophie: Great. So two workstreams today: one, confirm concurrency target that gives us best throughput while keeping p99 under 300ms; two, explore queuing/backpressure policy so bursts don't blow up latency.
[01:42] Daniel: On concurrency, our baseline tests show that for this model on H100 a concurrency of 4 gives steady latency but lower throughput; concurrency 8 increases tokens/sec ~1.6x but you start to see heavier tail. There's a sweet spot around 6 where throughput is ~1.4x and p99 still in range.
[02:01] Priya: How does that map to autoscaling? If we set concurrency to 6 per worker and target x workers, what is the burst behaviour?
[02:14] Daniel: We recommend configuring autoscale with a queue-depth threshold. If queue depth goes above 30 requests, spin up burst workers. The runtime supports fast spin-up for burst capacity - but note there's a cold-start window of ~20-40s depending on image warmness.
[02:33] Marcus: That cold-start is rough for our use-case. Can we maintain a small warm pool for peak hours?
[02:41] Sophie: Yes, Dedicated supports reserved warm capacity; we can size a minimal pool to cover baseline plus fast autoscale for spikes. We'll include cost tradeoffs in the follow-up SOW.
[02:54] Rachel: About queueing, what backpressure strategies are available? We don't want requests to pile up and then timeout downstream.
[03:06] Daniel: We have a couple: 1) early-reject at the gateway with a retry-after header; 2) priority queueing - user-critical requests get bumped; 3) dynamic admission using estimated cost per request so very long sequences can be rate-limited. For the POC I suggest priority + a soft queue limit to keep p99 stable.
[03:29] Priya: Sounds good. Can you explain continuous batching again — I'm still fuzzy on how it interacts with concurrency?
[03:37] Daniel: Sure. Continuous batching keeps worker GPUs accepting new tokens and concatenating sequences whenever possible so you don't wait for a full batch to form. That reduces average per-token overhead. However, it increases effective parallelism inside a worker so you need to tune concurrency: too high concurrency and the worker's memory/compute gets saturated leading to tail spikes.
[04:00] Daniel: Practically, we dial batching window and max batch size together. For our model we saw best results with window 15-25ms and max batch 64. With concurrency 6-8 on H100 we get peak throughput; but tune window down if p99 grows.
[04:18] Marcus: The Friday run used window 20ms maxbatch 128. Maybe that's why p99 spiked.
[04:26] Daniel: Exactly — large maxbatch helped throughput but increased variability. We'll retest with maxbatch 64.
[04:34] Rachel: Any instrumentation we should look at? I want to correlate incoming request size distribution to p99 events.
[04:42] Daniel: We'll provide per-request histograms, KV cache hit-rate, batching utilization, and per-GPU util. Also the runtime emits a batch-latency trace which shows time spent waiting for batch vs attention compute.
[04:59] Sophie: For the longer run we discussed - Daniel will run a one-hour continuous-batching test at concurrency 8 and also a 1hr at concurrency 6, both with maxbatch 64 and window 20ms so we can compare.
[05:14] Rachel: Do you mind if we run a small sample of our production traffic through the POC? Even anonymized sample would help.
[05:22] Sophie: Not at all, that's actually ideal. Marcus, is it feasible to extract a 24h anonymized trace?
[05:29] Marcus: Yes we can pull it but need to scrub PHI — we'll do it and share via the secure S3 link.
[05:36] Priya: On security, we also need to confirm VPC peering and KMS integration for the Dedicated pilot. Where are we with that?
[05:45] Sophie: We already shared the security pack; for the POC we can enable a customer VPC peering and KMS. I'll follow up with the infra sheet. That will be in the action items.
[05:55] Rachel: Back to perf: when you say H100, are you running the nvcr optimized kernels or the upstream runtime? We want to ensure the same kernel set in prod as POC.
[06:05] Daniel: We're using Redwood runtime with our tuned kernels for H100 — that is what we plan to replicate in Dedicated. We can export the kernel list for reproducibility.
[06:15] Rachel: Great. Also curious about quantization: Friday used q8, but how much gain do you see with q4? Is quality acceptable?
[06:24] Daniel: q4 reduces memory and increases batch capacity but can degrade some hallucination patterns; for throughput it's useful for larger models. For this model q8 was a safer balance. We can run a q4 trial on the longer run if you want to measure latency/quality tradeoff.
[06:38] Priya: Let's prioritize latency first — keep q8 for the base runs.
[06:43] Daniel: Understood. We'll keep q8.
[06:46] Sophie: Anything on cost expectations? Marcus mentioned burst capacity pricing last week.
[06:52] Marcus: Yes, we'd like a rough delta if we run reserved mini-pool + burst vs all-hosted with autoscale.
[06:59] Sophie: We'll add a cost sketch in the SOW. For now note that reserved capacity + small warm pool typically costs ~x1.4 of pure autoscale in our experience, but gives much better tail control. We'll quantify after we run the profling tests.
[07:14] Rachel: Let's talk accept criteria — for POC success we need sustained throughput to handle 50 RPS with median latency under 120ms and p99 under 300ms for 95% of test windows. Is that feasible?
[07:29] Daniel: From initial numbers, 50 RPS mapping to tokens/sec depends on average sequence length. If your average is 150 tokens, that's ~7.5k tokens/sec. H100 at concurrency 6-8 with caching should hit that. So yes, likely feasible with tuned config.
[07:46] Priya: We'll validate once you have the 1hr runs and we feed our traffic sample.
[07:52] Daniel: Sounds good. Also we'll include a test with the priority queue enabled to show how it keeps p99 stable under burst.
[08:01] Rachel: Any open risks?
[08:04] Daniel: Risk list: cache hit-rate variability, cold-starts for burst workers, and edge cases with very long sequences causing worker saturation. We'll monitor and set admission rules to mitigate.
[08:16] Marcus: On the cold-start, is there an option to pre-pull models into warm images to cut the 20-40s down?
[08:23] Daniel: Yes, warm images and keep-alive sockets reduce it significantly — we can prototype a warm-pool approach.
[08:30] Sophie: Recap of action items: Daniel run 1hr tests (8c and 6c) with maxbatch 64 and window 20ms; Marcus/Rachel share anonymized 24h trace; Sophie to send updated SOW and cost delta for reserved warm pool.
[08:48] Rachel: Cool, let's aim to reconvene after results — same time next week?
[08:53] Sophie: Yes, next sync 2026-12-09 same time. I'll send calendar invite.
[08:59] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[09:02] Sophie: Thanks, meeting adjourned.
